title: How the planets move
subtitle: Evening stars, morning stars, and planets that are up all night

sections.heading: Inside track: Mercury and Venus
body: After this lesson you will be able to say when and where to look for each planet from one fact about it: where it is in its orbit relative to the Sun and Earth.

Mercury and Venus orbit closer to the Sun than we do. Looking in from outside, we see them swing from one side of the Sun to the other and back. They can never be opposite the Sun in our sky, so from anywhere but the polar regions they are never up in the middle of the night.

When one of them is east of the Sun it sets after the Sun and shows in the western sky at dusk: an evening star. When it is west of the Sun it rises first and shows in the east before dawn: a morning star. The widest swing is called greatest elongation. For Venus that is about 46°, which keeps it up for three hours or more after sunset. For Mercury it is between 18° and 28°, never clear of twilight for long. In between, each planet passes behind the Sun or between us and the Sun and is lost in its glare.

Venus takes about 19 months to go through the whole cycle, with roughly eight months as an evening star and eight as a morning star. Mercury does it in under four months, so it has several short appearances a year.

demo.title: Venus either side of the Sun

steps.caption: March 22, 2028, 7:45 pm, looking west from mid-northern latitudes. Venus is at greatest elongation as an evening star, 46° from the Sun, which set half an hour ago. Step forward a month at a time and watch Venus sink back toward the Sun by June.

January 3, 2027, 6:15 am, looking southeast from mid-northern latitudes. Here Venus is at greatest elongation on the other side: 47° west of the Sun, rising more than three hours before it as the morning star.

figures.caption: Seen from Earth, an inner planet can only swing so far from the Sun before its path turns back: the sight line just grazes its orbit (green lines). East of the Sun it is an evening star, west of it a morning star. The telescope view shows why Galileo's observation of Venus's phases mattered: it goes from a small full disc beyond the Sun to a large thin crescent near us.

misconception.myth: The evening star and the morning star are two different stars.
misconception.fact: Both are usually Venus, a planet, seen on either side of the Sun at different times of its cycle. The ancient Greeks first gave them two names, Hesperus and Phosphorus, before realising they were the same object.

check.prompt: Venus is at greatest western elongation, 46° west of the Sun. When and where should you look for it?
choices: In the east before sunrise
In the west after sunset
High in the sky at midnight
It cannot be seen until it moves east of the Sun
check.explanation: West of the Sun means it rises before the Sun: a morning star, low in the east in the hours before dawn.

sections.heading: Outside track: Mars, Jupiter and Saturn
body: The planets beyond Earth can be anywhere along the ecliptic, including straight opposite the Sun. That moment is called opposition, and it is the best time to see an outer planet. It rises at sunset, is highest around midnight and sets at sunrise, so it is up all night. Earth is passing between it and the Sun, so it is also at its closest and brightest.

After opposition the planet rises earlier each night. For a few months it is an evening object, already up when darkness falls and setting earlier and earlier. Then it sinks into the sunset glow and passes behind the Sun. That is conjunction, when the planet is invisible for weeks. It reappears before dawn and slowly works its way back to the next opposition.

Earth is on the faster inside lane, so we come round to lap Jupiter every 13 months and Saturn every 12 and a half. Mars moves nearly as fast as we do and takes about 26 months to catch, which is why good views of Mars are rare.

demo.title: Mars at opposition: up all night

steps.caption: February 19, 2027, 6:30 pm, looking east from mid-northern latitudes. The Sun has just set behind you and Mars is coming up directly opposite it, with Jupiter above. The nearly full Moon happens to be right beside them tonight; a full Moon is at opposition too.
A quarter past midnight. Mars is due south (due north, from the southern hemisphere) and at its highest, 64° up, at the hour when the Sun is farthest below your feet.
6 am, looking west. Mars is going down as the eastern sky brightens. It has been up for the whole night.
The opposite case: Saturn at conjunction, midday on April 7, 2027, with the blue sky removed. Saturn is 2° from the Sun and cannot be seen at all for several weeks around this date.

figures.caption: Earth, on the inside lane, catches up with an outer planet and passes it at opposition, when the planet is opposite the Sun, up all night and closest. Slide through the cycle: the planet falls behind into the evening sky, passes behind the Sun at conjunction, and returns in the morning sky. Compare how long the cycle takes for Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.

thinkAbout.question: Could an astronaut on Mars ever see Earth high in the sky at midnight?
thinkAbout.answer: No. For Mars, Earth is an inner planet, just as Venus is for us. Earth would only ever appear as an evening or morning star, never more than about 40° from the Sun, and the brilliant blue 'star' of the Martian dawn or dusk sky would be us.

check.prompt: Saturn rises around midnight. About how far from the Sun is it in the sky, and where is it in its cycle?
choices: About 90° west of the Sun, heading toward opposition
About 90° east of the Sun, just after opposition
Opposite the Sun, at opposition
Close to the Sun, near conjunction
check.explanation: An object that rises six hours before the Sun is about 90° west of it: a morning object that will reach opposition in a few months as Earth catches up.

sections.heading: How fast they cross the zodiac
body: Against the stars, the outer planets usually creep eastward, the same direction as the Sun and Moon. Their speed depends on the size of their orbit. Mars goes around the Sun in just under two years and normally crosses a zodiac constellation in a month or two. Jupiter takes almost 12 years, so it spends about a year in each constellation: learn where it is this year and you know roughly where it will be next year, one constellation to the east. Saturn takes 29 and a half years and lingers in each constellation for two years or more.
Mercury and Venus, tied to the Sun, average the Sun's pace of one lap a year, darting ahead of it and falling behind.

figures.caption: The real positions of the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn round the zodiac, with Earth in the middle. The coloured arcs show a year's travel: the Sun goes all the way round, Mars covers several constellations, Jupiter about one and Saturn less than half of one. Play the years to watch Jupiter tick round like the hour hand of a slow clock.

thinkAbout.question: Mars normally crosses a zodiac constellation in a month or two. Why does it sometimes stay in the same one for half a year?
thinkAbout.answer: Around opposition it stops, backs up and turns again: its retrograde loop. In 2026–27 Mars spent months doubling back through Leo and Cancer. The next lesson explains why.

sections.tryIt: Find Jupiter or Saturn and note which zodiac constellation it is in and what time it rises. If it rises around sunset, it is near opposition and this is the month to look at it. If it is already in the west at dusk, catch it soon: it is heading for conjunction.

keyPoints: Mercury and Venus stay near the Sun: evening stars in the west after sunset or morning stars in the east before sunrise, widest at greatest elongation.
Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are best at opposition: opposite the Sun, up all night, closest and brightest.
Near conjunction a planet is behind the Sun and invisible for weeks.
Jupiter moves about one zodiac constellation a year; Saturn takes two years or more per constellation; Mars a month or two.

questions.prompt: Why is Venus never seen high in the sky at midnight from mid-latitudes?
choices: It is too faint by then
Its orbit is inside Earth's, so it never gets more than about 47° from the Sun
It only shines by reflected moonlight
It sets at the same time as the Sun every day
questions.explanation: An inner planet can only swing a limited angle either side of the Sun, so it is confined to the hours after sunset or before sunrise.

questions.prompt: Jupiter is at opposition tonight. When does it rise?
choices: Around sunrise
Around midnight
It does not rise
Around sunset
questions.explanation: At opposition a planet is opposite the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets, is highest at midnight and sets at sunrise.

questions.prompt: Why is an outer planet brightest at opposition?
choices: Earth is between it and the Sun, so it is at its closest to us
The planet is closest to the Sun then
It is full of reflected moonlight
The night is darker at midnight
questions.explanation: At opposition Earth is on the same side of the Sun as the planet, at the minimum distance for that lap.

questions.prompt: Jupiter is in Leo this year. Where will it most likely be three years from now?
choices: Still in Leo
Back in Cancer
About three zodiac constellations farther east
On the opposite side of the sky
questions.explanation: Jupiter takes nearly 12 years to circle the 12 traditional zodiac constellations, about one a year, moving east.

questions.prompt: What is happening when Saturn is at conjunction?
choices: It is opposite the Sun and up all night
It is on the far side of the Sun and hidden in its glare
It is passing in front of the Sun as a black dot
It is as far from the ecliptic as it can get
questions.explanation: At conjunction an outer planet lies beyond the Sun in the same direction, rising and setting with it.

questions.prompt: Venus is 40° east of the Sun. When and where do you look for it?
choices: In the east before sunrise
High in the sky at midnight
In the west after sunset
It cannot be seen
questions.explanation: East of the Sun means it follows the Sun across the sky and sets after it: an evening star in the west.
